## Purpose

This SOP describes the field determination of soil texture using the
texture-by-feel (ribbon) method. This rapid, equipment-free technique
classifies soil into one of 12 USDA textural classes based on how a
moistened soil sample behaves when formed into a ball, extruded into a
ribbon, and rubbed between the fingers [@thien1979;
@soilsurveystaff2017]. Field texturing provides an immediate estimate of
sand, silt, and clay content without laboratory analysis.

## Scope

- **Applies to:** Field characterization of mineral soils at all EA
  Program sites; preliminary texture assessment for soil sampling
  campaigns
- **Does not apply to:** Soils with very high organic matter content
  (\>20%, e.g., peat); quantitative particle size analysis (use the
  hydrometer method, SOP-L401); soils with large gravel or rock fragment
  content (assess the fine fraction only)
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites; can also be performed on
  samples brought back to the lab

## Responsibilities

| Role | Responsibility |
|:-------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI | Approve protocol, ensure training compliance |
| Field Lead | Coordinate sampling, verify observer calibration |
| Trained Personnel | Perform texture assessments, record results |
| New Students | Complete training and calibration exercise before independent use |

## Definitions

- **Clay:** The finest soil particle size class, with equivalent
  spherical diameter less than 0.002 mm; imparts stickiness,
  plasticity, and cohesion to the moist soil; forms a long, flexible
  ribbon when extruded between thumb and forefinger.
- **Loam:** A textural class with roughly balanced proportions of sand,
  silt, and clay; exhibits moderate ribbon length (25--50 mm), moderate
  grittiness, and moderate stickiness; the most common agricultural
  soil texture.
- **Plasticity:** The ability of moist soil to be molded and deformed
  without cracking or crumbling; highest in clay-rich soils; assessed
  by rolling soil into a thread between the palms.
- **Ribbon:** The flat, continuous strip extruded when moist soil is
  pushed between the thumb and forefinger; ribbon length is the primary
  diagnostic criterion in the field texture-by-feel method; longer
  ribbons indicate higher clay content.
- **Sand:** Soil mineral particles with equivalent spherical diameter
  0.05--2.0 mm; feels gritty between the fingers; does not form a
  ribbon; individual grains are visible to the naked eye.
- **Silt:** Soil mineral particles with equivalent spherical diameter
  0.002--0.05 mm; feels smooth and floury when dry; slippery and
  slightly plastic when moist; imparts a silky texture to the soil.
- **Texture class:** A USDA classification category (e.g., sandy loam,
  silt clay loam, clay) based on the relative percentages of sand, silt,
  and clay; determined from the USDA textural triangle and confirmed by
  laboratory hydrometer analysis (see
  [SOP-L401](../lab_sops/SOP-L401-texture-hydrometer.qmd)).
- **Water content (field):** The moisture status of the soil at the
  time of testing; texture-by-feel must be performed on soil adjusted
  to a defined moist or wet state to produce consistent results across
  operators.
  
## Safety and Hazards

::: callout-warning
### Hazards

- **Biological:** Soil-borne pathogens; wash hands thoroughly after
  handling soil
- **Chemical:** At contaminated sites, soil may contain heavy metals or
  other hazardous materials; wear gloves
- **Physical:** Standard field hazards (ticks, snakes, heat exposure)
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (recommended, especially at unknown or contaminated
  sites)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] Hand sanitizer or soap and water for post-handling cleanup

### Required Training

- [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd)

## Background

### Soil Particle Size Fractions

Soil texture is defined by the relative proportions of three mineral
particle size fractions [@soilsurveystaff2017]:

| Fraction | Diameter | Feel |
|:--------------------------|:--------------------------|:-----------------|
| **Sand** | 2.0--0.05 mm | Gritty; individual grains visible and felt between fingers |
| **Silt** | 0.05--0.002 mm | Smooth, floury, or silky; like rubbing flour or talc |
| **Clay** | \< 0.002 mm | Sticky when wet; plastic and moldable; stains fingers |

### The USDA Textural Triangle

The 12 USDA textural classes are defined by the percentages of sand,
silt, and clay. The texture-by-feel method estimates which class a soil
belongs to without measuring exact percentages.

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: USDA soil textural triangle diagram -->

<!-- Save as: images/usda_textural_triangle.png -->

<!-- Many public domain versions available from USDA-NRCS -->

### Why Field Texture Matters

- Determines water-holding capacity, drainage, and aeration
- Guides sampling strategy (e.g., different sample weights for carbon
  analysis; see SOP-L406)
- Informs the soil texture correction factor for nutrient extractions
  (see [SOP-L403](../lab_sops/SOP-L403-nitrate-ammonium-kcl.qmd))
- Rapid enough to characterize many points across a landscape in a
  single field day

## Required Materials

| Item                          | Notes                                     |
|:----------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Water bottle with squeeze top | For wetting soil incrementally            |
| Small ruler (cm)              | For measuring ribbon length               |
| Field data sheet              | Printed from Appendix A                   |
| Clipboard and pencil          | Mechanical pencil preferred               |
| GPS unit or smartphone        | For recording sample locations            |
| Trowel or soil knife          | For collecting subsurface samples         |
| Sealable plastic bags         | If bringing samples back for confirmation |
| Paper towels or rag           | For cleaning hands between samples        |

No specialized laboratory equipment is required.

## Estimated Time

| Task | Time |
|:----------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Per sample (experienced observer) | 2--5 minutes |
| Per sample (new observer) | 5--10 minutes |
| Calibration exercise (training) | 30--45 minutes with known-texture standards |

## Procedure

### Collect the Sample

1.  Select a representative location and record GPS coordinates
2.  Clear surface litter and organic debris
3.  Collect approximately a golf-ball-sized amount of mineral soil from
    the target depth (typically 0--15 cm)
4.  Remove visible roots, gravel, and organic fragments

### Moisten the Sample

1.  Place the soil in your palm
2.  Add water drop by drop from the squeeze bottle while kneading the
    soil
3.  Continue adding water and kneading until the soil reaches the
    consistency of modeling clay or putty
4.  The soil should be uniformly moist but not dripping wet
5.  Crush all aggregates between your fingers during kneading

::: callout-important
### Getting the Moisture Right

This is the most critical step. If the soil is too dry, it will crumble
and you'll underestimate clay content. If too wet, it will be slippery
and you'll overestimate clay. The target is a smooth, pliable
consistency similar to play dough. This may take 2--3 minutes of
kneading.
:::

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: Series of 3 photos: dry soil in palm, adding water, properly kneaded bolus -->

<!-- Save as: images/soil_texture_moistening.jpg -->

### Test 1: Form a Ball

1.  Try to form the moistened soil into a ball (bolus) by squeezing and
    rolling in your palm
2.  **If the soil will not form a ball**, it is **Sand**. Record and
    move to the next sample.
3.  If a ball forms, proceed to Test 2

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: Photo of a properly formed soil ball in the palm -->

<!-- Save as: images/soil_texture_ball.jpg -->

### Test 2: Ribbon Test

1.  Place the ball between your thumb and forefinger
2.  Gently push the soil forward with your thumb, squeezing it into a
    flat ribbon about 2 mm thick and 1 cm wide
3.  Let the ribbon extend over your forefinger, unsupported, until it
    breaks from its own weight
4.  Measure the ribbon length with a ruler before it breaks
5.  Repeat 3--5 times and use the longest consistent ribbon

**Ribbon length determines clay content:**

| Ribbon Length           | Clay Content | Category          |
|:------------------------|:-------------|:------------------|
| No ribbon forms         | \< 10%       | Low clay          |
| \< 2.5 cm (\< 1 inch)   | 10--20%      | Low-moderate clay |
| 2.5--5 cm (1--2 inches) | 20--35%      | Moderate clay     |
| \> 5 cm (\> 2 inches)   | \> 35%       | High clay         |

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: Photo sequence of thumb extruding a ribbon over the forefinger, with a ruler alongside -->

<!-- Save as: images/soil_texture_ribbon.jpg -->

### Test 3: Feel Test (Grittiness and Smoothness)

1.  Take a pea-sized piece of the moistened soil
2.  Place it in your palm and add excess water to make a muddy slurry
3.  Rub the slurry between your thumb and forefinger using a circular
    motion
4.  Classify the dominant feel:

| Feel | Sensation | Dominant Fraction |
|:-----------------|:-------------------|:---------------------------------|
| **Gritty** | Like rubbing sugar or fine sand between fingers; individual grains felt and possibly heard | Sand-dominated |
| **Smooth** | Like rubbing flour or talc; silky, no grains felt | Silt-dominated |
| **Neither** | Neither gritty nor silky dominates; sticky | Sand and silt balanced |

### Determine Textural Class

Combine the ribbon length and feel test results using the following
decision matrix [@thien1979]:

|               | Gritty Feel     | Smooth Feel     | Neither Gritty nor Smooth |
|:---------------|:---------------|:---------------|:-----------------------|
| **No ribbon** | Sand            | Silt            | Loam                      |
| **\< 2.5 cm** | Sandy loam      | Silt loam       | Loam                      |
| **2.5--5 cm** | Sandy clay loam | Silty clay loam | Clay loam                 |
| **\> 5 cm**   | Sandy clay      | Silty clay      | Clay                      |

::: callout-tip
### Additional Clues

- **Loamy sand** falls between sand and sandy loam: barely forms a ball,
  very gritty, ribbon \<1 cm
- **Silt** (pure): very smooth, almost soapy when wet, forms a weak ball
  but no ribbon
- When in doubt between two classes, record both (e.g., "sandy loam /
  loam") and note the uncertainty
:::

### Record Results

Record the textural class, ribbon length, feel, and any notes on the
field data sheet (Appendix A). Photograph the ribbon if possible for
documentation.

## Supplementary Test: Jar Sedimentation

For a semi-quantitative confirmation of field texture, you can perform a
jar test on the same soil:

1.  Fill a clear, straight-sided jar (mason jar or pasta sauce jar)
    one-third full with soil
2.  Fill the jar with water, leaving 2 cm of headspace
3.  Add a pinch of non-foaming dish soap (dispersing agent)
4.  Cap tightly and shake vigorously for 2 minutes
5.  Set the jar on a level surface and do not disturb
6.  After 1 minute, mark the settled layer on the jar (this is **sand**)
7.  After 2 hours, mark the next layer (this is **silt**)
8.  After 24--48 hours, the remaining suspended material has settled
    (this is **clay**); the water above may still be slightly turbid
9.  Measure the thickness of each layer and calculate approximate
    percentages

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: Photo of a jar test at 48 hours showing distinct sand, silt, and clay layers marked on the glass -->

<!-- Save as: images/soil_texture_jar_test.jpg -->

::: callout-note
The jar test provides a rough visual estimate only. For precise particle
size distribution, use the hydrometer method (SOP-L401).
:::

## Quality Control

- **Calibration:** Before independent fieldwork, each observer must
  practice on at least 5 soils of known texture (confirmed by hydrometer
  analysis). Results should match the confirmed texture class for at
  least 4 of 5 samples.
- **Inter-observer agreement:** When multiple observers are surveying,
  have each observer independently classify at least 10% of the same
  samples. Agreement should be within one textural class. Inter-observer
  variability is a well-documented limitation of texture-by-feel;
  training and calibration reduce but do not eliminate systematic
  differences among observers [@salley2018].
- **Documentation:** Record ribbon length to the nearest 0.5 cm, not
  just the textural class, so results can be reviewed later.
- **Confirmation:** For critical projects, bring duplicate samples back
  to the lab for hydrometer analysis on at least 10% of field-textured
  samples.

When texture-by-feel results will inform quantitative analyses (e.g.,
pedotransfer functions for water-holding capacity), confirm at least 10%
of field-textured samples with hydrometer analysis
([SOP-L401](../lab_sops/SOP-L401-texture-hydrometer.qmd)). The accuracy
of the feel method varies by textural class: sandy and clayey soils are
identified most reliably, while loams and silt loams are misclassified
more often [@salley2018].

## Data Management

Enter results from field sheets into the project spreadsheet within 48
hours. Required fields:

- Date, site, plot ID, observer
- GPS coordinates
- Sample depth (cm)
- Ribbon length (cm)
- Feel (gritty, smooth, or neither)
- Textural class
- Notes (e.g., high gravel content, high organic matter, very dry)

## Training Record

Before performing field texture assessments independently, personnel
must:

1.  Read this SOP in full
2.  Complete a calibration exercise on at least 5 soils of known texture
3.  Demonstrate the moistening, ball, ribbon, and feel tests under
    supervision
4.  Achieve agreement within one textural class on 4 of 5 known samples
5.  Be signed off by the field lead or PI
